description: Somos un grupo de estudiantes universitarios unidos por el interés en la tecnología, la ciencia y la innovación. Participamos en el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 con el objetivo de crear soluciones creativas, funcionales y fáciles de entender a partir de datos reales de la NASA.
summary: Earth Jukebox is an accessible web app that turns NASA Earth science visuals into sound. Much of the Earth Information Center’s content is visual, which leaves blind and low-vision people without access to it. Our project has two prototypes. The Ocean Archive plays one year of NASA’s ECCO2 ocean currents and temperature video (March 2007 to March 2008): a Python script converts each frame’s color into an estimated temperature, and the page plays the Northern Hemisphere in the left ear and the Southern in the right, with a pulse that speeds up as more warm water appears. The Interactive Globe is a 3D instrument where users paint temperature anomalies and hear them as chords. A sound legend and screen-reader narration explain what each sound means. It is an educational tool, not a measurement instrument, and it opens the planet’s seasonal patterns to students, educators and everyone who cannot see them.
details:
What it does: Earth Jukebox has two modules. In the Ocean Archive, we analyze NASA SVS 3912 (ECCO2 surface currents colored by temperature, March 2007 to March 2008) frame by frame with Python, OpenCV and NumPy. Each pixel color is converted to an estimated temperature using NASA’s color bar, averaged for the northern and southern halves of the map, and saved to a data.json file. The web page reads it in sync with the video and plays two synthesized voices: North in the left ear, South in the right. A low pulse beats faster when more of the ocean is at 25 °C or above. In the Interactive Globe, users paint temperature anomalies on a 3D Earth (base layer from NASA SVS 5196, DYAMOND CO₂) with a Thermal Brush, and the sound engine plays them as chords: cold zones as deep minor chords, hot zones as brighter major chords, adjustable by scale and style.

Benefits and impact: Most Earth science is communicated through maps and animations that blind and low-vision people cannot use. Earth Jukebox offers another way in, with screen-reader narration, a sound legend and keyboard-friendly controls, and it can help students, educators and museums explain seasons and climate through hearing.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js (3D globe), Tone.js and the Web Audio API (sound), Python with OpenCV and NumPy (data), GitHub Pages (hosting), Canva (slides).

Creativity: We turn a year of ocean data into a stereo piece where each hemisphere is an ear, and we turn a globe into an instrument. Sound is tied to the data, not used as decoration.

What we considered: Temperatures are estimated from video color, not measured, and ECCO2 is a model covering one year. The note scale is stretched to the video’s minimum and maximum so small changes are audible. The globe uses user-painted values, not NASA measurements. Data: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, SVS 3912 and 5196. AI disclosure: Claude (Anthropic) helped write code and text
dataRefs: Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature
